questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — ticket booking with holds (javabootcamp System Design, guide astraupskill/03-SYSTEM-DESIGN.md §4.4; blocks from modules 10, 12 and 13). Requirements: many people try to buy the same seats at the same moment; a seat is sold at most once; a user can hold seats for ten minutes while paying; unpaid holds expire; payment must not be charged twice. Write your design before you look: sizing, data model, partitioning, consistency and concurrency control, failure modes, and the trade-off you would defend. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70 % with every [w3] hit).

keyPoints.text: [w2] Size the on-sale spike, not the average day: flash sales put a rate limit and a queue in front of the whole booking path.
[w3] Data model: a seats store with a version per seat (or per section), and a hold recorded as seat -> (user, expiresAt).
[w3] 'At most once per seat' is a compare-and-set on the seat's version: read it with its version and write back only if the version is unchanged, so of two buyers only the first write wins.
keyPoints.quote: read a row with its version, compute, write back only if the version has not changed

keyPoints.text: [w2] The hold is a lease with an expiry on an injected clock, and its expiry is a delayed job.
[w3] Payment is idempotent (Idempotency-Key), and booking across inventory and payment is a saga: hold, charge, confirm, and on failure release the hold and refund.
[w1] Partitioning follows the access pattern: listing bookings by date suits range partitioning.

[w3] Concurrency regime stated: optimistic locking shines when conflicts are rare, but at a popular on-sale every buyer conflicts on the same sections, where a short pessimistic lock or a single-writer queue per event can be better.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same booking system at 10x the on-sale traffic, or with the payment provider slow or down. What breaks first, and what in your design already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Under heavy contention optimistic retries waste work and pile up into a retry storm; that is the regime where a real lock or a queue wins.
keyPoints.quote: under heavy contention the retries waste work and a real lock is better

keyPoints.text: [w3] The hold expires at the very moment payment confirms: both the confirm and the release must be conditional writes ('still held by this hold id'), or the expiry job frees a seat that was just sold.
[w2] A slow provider makes clients retry 'pay': every retry needs a story for 'what if the first attempt actually succeeded?'.
[w2] A paused holder does not know its lease has run out, so hold expiry cannot trust wall-clock time alone; leases need margins and fencing tokens.
keyPoints.quote: Because a paused leader does not know its lease ran out

keyPoints.text: [w1] The refund (a compensation) can fail too: compensations are retried and must be idempotent, and a saga that runs out of retries must report itself stuck.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your booking choices against the alternatives the guide names. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Saga, not two-phase commit with the payment provider: external providers do not join your transactions and 2PC blocks while the coordinator is unsure; the saga trades isolation (others briefly see 'held') for availability.
[w2] Why 2PC blocks: a participant that voted YES keeps its locks until it learns the decision.
keyPoints.quote: a participant that voted YES holds its locks until it hears the decision

keyPoints.text: [w2] Choosing pessimistic locks instead brings deadlocks and locks held by dead clients, so they need timeouts or leases.
[w2] Seats are on the strong side of the consistency table (inventory, uniqueness): during a partition the minority side refuses rather than double-selling.

[w1] Know the store's isolation level: snapshot isolation (MVCC) still allows write skew, where two transactions read the same rows and write different ones; only serializable rules it out, so the answer says which level the seats store runs at.
keyPoints.quote: write skew: two transactions read the same rows and write different ones
